edits.before: Climate mitigation scenarios that treat sustainable aviation fuel as a unified category may overlook whether infrastructure deployed for near-term pathways transfers to deeper-decarbonization successors. We examine this question by optimizing full supply chains for 13 carbon–hydrogen–route combinations serving Beijing and Tianjin airports over four representative weeks. The cost–emission comparison reveals pronounced cost differences: natural-gas-to-liquids costs 6.50 yuan/kg at 100% demand coverage, compared with 26.06 yuan/kg and 43.84% coverage for captured industrial carbon and green hydrogen converted through Fischer–Tropsch synthesis. Spatially, the demand-driven network of the fossil pathway and the resource-driven network of the green-hydrogen pathway differ upstream but show partial synthesis-site overlap; capacity matched within 25 km represents 23.8% and 47.8% of their respective installed synthesis capacities. Operationally, both pathways have utilization-based capacity premiums dominated by the worst-week component, while the green-hydrogen pathway additionally exhibits low hydrogen-production utilization. These linked differences in cost, geography and operations show that synthetic aviation-fuel pathway switching can involve industrial regime reconstruction, even where some synthesis locations are shared. Net-zero scenarios therefore need to account explicitly for pathway-specific infrastructure transitions to avoid overstating how near-term deployment supports later aviation decarbonization.

edits.paragraph_after: To test this hypothesis, we compiled techno-economic, lifecycle and process parameters for 13 carbon–hydrogen–route combinations (retained pathway set and activation matrix in Tables S6–S7; techno-economic, lifecycle, and process parameters in Tables S8–S9), together with renewable power output series. Ethanol–alcohol-to-jet co-location27, ethanol-to-jet techno-economic and lifecycle assessment28, and Fischer–Tropsch versus methanol-to-jet plant comparison29 provide context for route-specific process configurations. Four representative weeks selected from airport demand were used for comparative optimization. Demand coverage diagnostics are shown in Figs. S4–S5 and Table S2; Table S26 evaluates their joint demand–renewable coverage against the twelve-week resource pool. We then developed a multi-commodity flow programming framework that integrates a three-layer production–transport–consumption network with three-hour production and inventory decisions, commodity-specific transport time scales and weekly airport-demand decisions, jointly optimizing facility siting, capacity planning, inventory scheduling, and demand fulfilment for Beijing and Tianjin airports within a mainland-China resource search domain. An overview of this cost-driven mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) framework is provided in Fig. S19. In the pathway labels, GTL denotes natural-gas-to-liquids, BH industrial by-product hydrogen, GH green hydrogen, FT Fischer–Tropsch synthesis, CCU industrial carbon capture and utilization, DAC direct air capture, and MTJ methanol-to-jet. edits.before: Cost changes along the frontier show a pronounced step at the captured-carbon–green-hydrogen combination. From GTL-BH to GTL, unit cost rises only from 5.29 to 6.50 CNY/kg (approximately 0.74 and 0.91 USD/kg), a modest change while both meet all demand and GTL remains within the assumed 6–8 CNY/kg price range. The comparison between GTL and CCU-GH-FT shows a more pronounced cost step: CCU-GH-FT costs 29.61 CNY/kg (approximately 4.15 USD/kg), about four times the GTL unit cost, while supplying 47.02% of demand (Figure 1a,b). The bend in the frontier at this point therefore reflects changes in both cost and supplied quantity. The lower-cost full-supply and higher-cost partial-supply configurations rely on different carbon and hydrogen sources and associated facilities, indicating that this cost step involves structural differences between production systems.

edits.before: The differences among frontier pathways extend from production structure to the spatial organization of physical infrastructure. Figure 2 compares the compact GTL network, the cross-regional GTL-BH network and the resource-dependent CCU-GH-FT network, with the dispersed DAC-BH-FT configuration providing a spatial comparator. Their feedstock sourcing, facility distributions and transport connections follow different organizing principles. At the same time, GTL and CCU-GH-FT retain some synthesis capacity at common demand locations. These configurations connect distinct upstream networks with varying degrees of synthesis-site correspondence, making both dimensions relevant to infrastructure inheritability.

edits.before: A counterintuitive starting point is that pathways with identical node counts can follow entirely opposite spatial logics. GTL-BH and GTL both comprise four positive-flow network identifiers and two physical synthesis sites, yet their spatial organization principles diverge sharply. GTL-BH has a cross-regional logistics ratio of 77.47% and a quantity-weighted fuel-transport distance of 135.25 km (Figure 2c,g,k). Its low-cost position relies on long-distance logistics connecting a small number of facilities. GTL presents a nearly opposite spatial profile. Its cross-regional logistics ratio drops to 0%, with synthesis located at the two airport coordinates, forming a local production–demand structure (Figure 2b,f,j). Production and demand share the same airport sites, and the levelized cost of 6.50 CNY/kg lies within the market-price range. Both pathways comprise four network identifiers, yet GTL-BH follows a compressed cross-regional pattern while GTL follows a proximal closed-loop pattern. Identical node counts mask a fundamental divergence in spatial logic. Scenario-level spatial and network indicators for all 13 pathways are summarized in Table S18, and pathway-specific transport-route maps are provided in the Supplementary Archive (Figs. S49–S63).
edits.after: GTL-BH and GTL organize production and delivery differently. GTL-BH comprises 34 positive-flow network identifiers and 2 physical synthesis sites. Its 30 hydrogen-conditioning modules support airport synthesis; the cross-regional logistics ratio is 4.20%, with quantity-weighted hydrogen and fuel transport distances of 131.61 and 0.00 km, respectively (Figure 2c,g,k). GTL comprises 4 network identifiers and 2 physical synthesis sites, with a cross-regional logistics ratio of 0.00% and mean fuel-transport distance of 0.00 km (Figure 2b,f,j). GTL places synthesis at the two airport coordinates and meets 100.00% of demand at 6.50 CNY/kg. These configurations show how feedstock and process choices change the network supporting the same airport demand. edits.before: The spatial expansion of CCU-GH-FT reorganizes hydrogen production and synthesis around dispersed renewable resources. Compared with GTL, which organizes synthesis at two airport sites, this configuration distributes hydrogen production and synthesis across multiple locations: it contains 129 positive-flow network identifiers, 109 hydrogen-production records and 71 synthesis modules at 57 physical coordinates (Figure 2a,e,i). Production at these locations is connected mainly through relatively short commodity flows, with mean hydrogen and fuel transport distances of 63.51 and 32.22 km, respectively, and only 3.23% of mass flow travelling more than 100 km. The network expansion thus centres on reorganizing facility locations and transport connections around resource sourcing. With 49,128 kg/h of synthesis capacity, this configuration meets 47.02% of demand while retaining some synthesis capacity at the airport demand sites, linking a dispersed upstream resource network to continuing demand-side locations. Resource distribution and demand geography therefore jointly shape the spatial organization of this pathway (Table S18 and Figs. S27 and S57).

edits.before: Spatial dispersion alone does not ensure cost–emission competitiveness in the configurations examined. DAC-BH-FT lies outside the nondominated set in Figure 1a despite its dispersed synthesis layout. It contains 28 positive-flow network identifiers and 26 synthesis modules at 26 physical coordinates. Its 26 generic hydrogen-facility records represent the configured supply or purification modules, and no positive explicit hydrogen-route flow is recorded. The quantity-weighted fuel-transport distance is 150.85 km, and 56.94% of the aggregate hydrogen, CO₂ and fuel mass flow travels more than 100 km (Table S18; Figure 2d,h,l). This combination of a dispersed layout, long delivery distances and a dominated cost–emission position shows why facility dispersion is an insufficient indicator of pathway performance. The full DAC-BH-FT transport-route map is provided in the Supplementary Archive (Fig. S63).

The quantity-weighted fuel-transport distance is 167.46 km, and 58.17% of aggregate hydrogen, CO₂ and fuel mass flow travels more than 100 km (Table S18; Figure 2d,h,l). Facility dispersion, transport requirements and performance at the achieved service level therefore need to be considered together. edits.before: CCU-GH-FT extends the operating challenge from week-to-week synthesis output to coordination between hydrogen production and fuel synthesis. Mean H₂ utilization is 27.65% and mean fuel-synthesis utilization is 72.71% (Figure 3a). Along the renewable-power-to-electrolysis-to-fuel-synthesis chain, a lightly utilized hydrogen-production stage therefore supports a more heavily utilized synthesis stage, while synthesis output also contracts markedly in the worst week. Its operating requirements consequently encompass both upstream capacity use and the timing of fuel production.

edits.before: Our analysis shows that synthetic aviation-fuel pathway switching can involve reorganization of supply-chain architecture across cost structure, spatial configuration, and temporal-operational requirements. Pathways that appear adjacent within a shared SAF category do not necessarily share compatible upstream resource bases, network topologies, or operating logics. In the Beijing–Tianjin case, GTL organizes synthesis at airport locations and meets all demand, whereas CCU-GH-FT connects distributed upstream resources to synthesis capacity partly located at the same demand sites. Under the stated resource conditions, CCU-GH-FT meets 47.02% of demand and combines low electrolyser utilization with a large additional synthesis-capacity premium associated with the worst week. The coexistence of shared synthesis locations and different upstream requirements makes infrastructure inheritability a question about particular production and supply functions. Early low-cost capacity can become exposed to stranding if its resource connections and production equipment cannot support later pathways.

edits.paragraph_after: The central implication is that early SAF investment needs to be judged by its ability to support later production systems as well as its current cost and supply. Even within a shared synthetic aviation-fuel category, changing carbon and hydrogen sources can require reorganization of the industrial system through which fuel is produced and delivered. The GTL–CCU-GH-FT comparison shows that partial geographic continuity at the synthesis stage can coexist with different upstream supply networks and operating requirements. A shared demand-side synthesis site provides geographic opportunities for continuity, while hydrogen and carbon supply and their temporal coordination remain pathway-specific. Assessing infrastructure inheritability therefore means identifying which sites and logistics can be retained, which production functions require adaptation, and where investment may become locked into facilities with limited subsequent uses.

edits.paragraph_after: To represent spatial heterogeneity, we constructed a multi-commodity flow network comprising georeferenced hydrogen sources, carbon sources, candidate production plants, and airports. Spatial resolution is at the facility or resource-site level, using point coordinates and candidate transport links. The resource search domain is mainland China, while fuel demand is restricted to Beijing and Tianjin airports. To limit model size, candidate transport links were screened using a maximum-distance threshold and a nearest-neighbour rule; scenario- and commodity-specific screening distances are reported in the Supplementary Information (Tables S3 and S10). The comparative runs represent four weeks (weeks 1, 5, 14 and 44), totalling 672 hours and 224 three-hour periods. Production and inventory decisions use the three-hour periods. Hydrogen deliveries in the recomputed configurations are balanced at both ends of each three-hour interval and sum to a common route-specific volume in each week. GTL-GH and GTL-BH natural-gas deliveries satisfy 28 daily balances, with eight periods per day. Airport deliveries and demand are weekly. Carbon supply options included coal-chemical sources, natural-gas-chemical sources, industrial capture, and direct air capture (DAC). Hydrogen supply options included green hydrogen, by-product hydrogen, and grey hydrogen, which were activated or deactivated through scenario-specific indicator parameters. Two synthesis routes were considered: Fischer–Tropsch (FT) and methanol-to-jet (MTJ) 29 (route-module activation assumptions in Table S5; feedstock, process, and capture parameters in Table S9); the MTJ route explicitly includes methanol intermediate inventory. Capacity, material-flow and inventory limits are enforced, and shortage variables report unmet demand. The baseline CTL case cannot satisfy its 90% minimum-production requirement under the available resources: the necessary resource bound is 78.6147%. A partial-supply diagnostic removes that inequality while retaining all other constraints; its production assets are fixed for the alternative-week test, which uses the same diagnostic service scope.

edits.before: Climate mitigation scenarios that treat sustainable aviation fuel as a unified category may overlook whether infrastructure deployed for near-term pathways transfers to deeper-decarbonization successors. We examine this question by optimizing full supply chains for 13 carbon–hydrogen–route combinations serving Beijing and Tianjin airports over four representative weeks. The cost–emission comparison reveals pronounced cost differences: natural-gas-to-liquids costs 6.50 yuan/kg at 100% demand coverage, compared with 26.06 yuan/kg and 43.84% coverage for captured industrial carbon and green hydrogen converted through Fischer–Tropsch synthesis. Spatially, the demand-driven network of the fossil pathway and the resource-driven network of the green-hydrogen pathway differ upstream but show partial synthesis-site overlap; capacity matched within 25 km represents 23.8% and 47.8% of their respective installed synthesis capacities. Operationally, both pathways have utilization-based capacity premiums dominated by the worst-week component, while the green-hydrogen pathway additionally exhibits low hydrogen-production utilization. These linked differences in cost, geography and operations show that synthetic aviation-fuel pathway switching can involve industrial regime reconstruction, even where some synthesis locations are shared. Net-zero scenarios therefore need to account explicitly for pathway-specific infrastructure transitions to avoid overstating how near-term deployment supports later aviation decarbonization.

edits.before: The differences among frontier pathways extend from production structure to the spatial organization of physical infrastructure. Figure 2 compares the compact GTL network, the cross-regional GTL-BH network and the resource-dependent CCU-GH-FT network, with the dispersed DAC-BH-FT configuration providing a spatial comparator. Their feedstock sourcing, facility distributions and transport connections follow different organizing principles. At the same time, GTL and CCU-GH-FT retain some synthesis capacity at common demand locations. These configurations connect distinct upstream networks with varying degrees of synthesis-site correspondence, making both dimensions relevant to infrastructure inheritability.

edits.before: A counterintuitive starting point is that pathways with identical node counts can follow entirely opposite spatial logics. GTL-BH and GTL both comprise four positive-flow network identifiers and two physical synthesis sites, yet their spatial organization principles diverge sharply. GTL-BH has a cross-regional logistics ratio of 77.47% and a quantity-weighted fuel-transport distance of 135.25 km (Figure 2c,g,k). Its low-cost position relies on long-distance logistics connecting a small number of facilities. GTL presents a nearly opposite spatial profile. Its cross-regional logistics ratio drops to 0%, with synthesis located at the two airport coordinates, forming a local production–demand structure (Figure 2b,f,j). Production and demand share the same airport sites, and the levelized cost of 6.50 CNY/kg lies within the market-price range. Both pathways comprise four network identifiers, yet GTL-BH follows a compressed cross-regional pattern while GTL follows a proximal closed-loop pattern. Identical node counts mask a fundamental divergence in spatial logic. Scenario-level spatial and network indicators for all 13 pathways are summarized in Table S18, and pathway-specific transport-route maps are provided in the Supplementary Archive (Figs. S49–S63).
edits.after: GTL-BH and GTL organize production and delivery differently. GTL-BH comprises 34 positive-flow network identifiers and 2 physical synthesis sites. GTL comprises 4 network identifiers and 2 physical synthesis sites, with a cross-regional logistics ratio of 0.00% and mean fuel-transport distance of 0.00 km (Figure 2b,f,j). GTL places synthesis at the two airport coordinates and meets 100.00% of demand at 6.50 CNY/kg. edits.before: The spatial expansion of CCU-GH-FT reorganizes hydrogen production and synthesis around dispersed renewable resources. Compared with GTL, which organizes synthesis at two airport sites, this configuration distributes hydrogen production and synthesis across multiple locations: it contains 129 positive-flow network identifiers, 109 hydrogen-production records and 71 synthesis modules at 57 physical coordinates (Figure 2a,e,i). Production at these locations is connected mainly through relatively short commodity flows, with mean hydrogen and fuel transport distances of 63.51 and 32.22 km, respectively, and only 3.23% of mass flow travelling more than 100 km. The network expansion thus centres on reorganizing facility locations and transport connections around resource sourcing. With 49,128 kg/h of synthesis capacity, this configuration meets 47.02% of demand while retaining some synthesis capacity at the airport demand sites, linking a dispersed upstream resource network to continuing demand-side locations. Resource distribution and demand geography therefore jointly shape the spatial organization of this pathway (Table S18 and Figs. S27 and S57).

edits.before: Spatial dispersion alone does not ensure cost–emission competitiveness in the configurations examined. DAC-BH-FT lies outside the nondominated set in Figure 1a despite its dispersed synthesis layout. It contains 28 positive-flow network identifiers and 26 synthesis modules at 26 physical coordinates. Its 26 generic hydrogen-facility records represent the configured supply or purification modules, and no positive explicit hydrogen-route flow is recorded. The quantity-weighted fuel-transport distance is 150.85 km, and 56.94% of the aggregate hydrogen, CO₂ and fuel mass flow travels more than 100 km (Table S18; Figure 2d,h,l). edits.before: Our analysis shows that synthetic aviation-fuel pathway switching can involve reorganization of supply-chain architecture across cost structure, spatial configuration, and temporal-operational requirements. Pathways that appear adjacent within a shared SAF category do not necessarily share compatible upstream resource bases, network topologies, or operating logics. In the Beijing–Tianjin case, GTL organizes synthesis at airport locations and meets all demand, whereas CCU-GH-FT connects distributed upstream resources to synthesis capacity partly located at the same demand sites. Under the stated resource conditions, CCU-GH-FT meets 47.02% of demand and combines low electrolyser utilization with a large additional synthesis-capacity premium associated with the worst week. The coexistence of shared synthesis locations and different upstream requirements makes infrastructure inheritability a question about particular production and supply functions. Early low-cost capacity can become exposed to stranding if its resource connections and production equipment cannot support later pathways.

edits.paragraph_after: The central implication is that early SAF investment needs to be judged by its ability to support later production systems as well as its current cost and supply. Even within a shared synthetic aviation-fuel category, changing carbon and hydrogen sources can require reorganization of the industrial system through which fuel is produced and delivered. The GTL–CCU-GH-FT comparison shows that partial geographic continuity at the synthesis stage can coexist with different upstream supply networks and operating requirements. A shared demand-side synthesis site provides geographic opportunities for continuity, while hydrogen and carbon supply and their temporal coordination remain pathway-specific. Assessing infrastructure inheritability therefore means identifying which sites and logistics can be retained, which production functions require adaptation, and where investment may become locked into facilities with limited subsequent uses.

edits.paragraph_after: To represent spatial heterogeneity, we constructed a multi-commodity flow network comprising georeferenced hydrogen sources, carbon sources, candidate production plants, and airports. Spatial resolution is at the facility or resource-site level, using point coordinates and candidate transport links. The resource search domain is mainland China, while fuel demand is restricted to Beijing and Tianjin airports. To limit model size, candidate transport links were screened using a maximum-distance threshold and a nearest-neighbour rule; scenario- and commodity-specific screening distances are reported in the Supplementary Information (Tables S3 and S10). The comparative runs represent four weeks (weeks 1, 5, 14 and 44), totalling 672 hours and 224 three-hour periods. Production and inventory decisions use the three-hour periods. Hydrogen deliveries in the recomputed configurations are balanced at both ends of each three-hour interval and sum to a common route-specific volume in each week. GTL-GH and GTL-BH natural-gas deliveries satisfy 28 daily balances, with eight periods per day. Airport deliveries and demand are weekly. Carbon supply options included coal-chemical sources, natural-gas-chemical sources, industrial capture, and direct air capture (DAC). Hydrogen supply options included green hydrogen, by-product hydrogen, and grey hydrogen, which were activated or deactivated through scenario-specific indicator parameters. Two synthesis routes were considered: Fischer–Tropsch (FT) and methanol-to-jet (MTJ) 29 (route-module activation assumptions in Table S5; feedstock, process, and capture parameters in Table S9); the MTJ route explicitly includes methanol intermediate inventory. Capacity, material-flow and inventory limits are enforced, and shortage variables report unmet demand. The baseline CTL case cannot satisfy its 90% minimum-production requirement under the available resources: the necessary resource bound is 78.6147%. A partial-supply diagnostic removes that inequality while retaining all other constraints; its production assets are fixed for the alternative-week test, which uses the same diagnostic service scope.

edits.before: The optimization model was implemented in Python. Six electricity-dependent configurations were evaluated with COPT 8.0.7 using full-model feasible schedules and valid lower bounds from a routing projection. All twelve baseline and fixed-production-design alternative-week solutions meet a 1% total-objective-gap criterion; the largest achieved gap is 0.7284%. edits.before: 气候减缓情景将可持续航空燃料作为统一类别时，可能忽略近期路径所部署的基础设施能否延续用于更深度脱碳的后续路径。本研究通过优化四个代表周内为北京和天津机场供油的13种碳源—氢源—工艺路线组合的完整供应链，考察这一问题。成本—排放比较显示出显著的成本差异：天然气制液体燃料的成本为6.50元/kg，满足全部需求；工业捕集碳与绿氢结合的费托路径成本为26.06元/kg，需求满足率为43.84%。空间上，化石路径的需求驱动网络与绿氢路径的资源驱动网络在上游存在差异，同时具有部分合成厂址重合；25 km阈值内的匹配产能分别占两种配置合成产能的23.8%和47.8%。运行上，两条路径基于利用率计算的容量溢价均以最差周分量为主，绿氢路径还表现出制氢端利用率较低的特征。成本、地理与运行方面的联动差异表明，合成航空燃料路径切换可能涉及产业格局重构，即使存在部分合成厂址重合。因此，净零情景需要显式纳入这些路径间的基础设施转换需求，避免高估近期部署对后续航空脱碳的支撑作用。

edits.paragraph_after: 为表示空间异质性，我们构建了由具有地理坐标的氢源、碳源、候选生产设施和机场组成的多商品流网络。空间分辨率为设施或资源站点尺度，采用点位坐标与候选运输连接。资源搜索范围为中国大陆，燃料需求限于北京和天津机场。为控制模型规模，候选运输连接采用最大距离阈值与最近邻规则筛选；不同情景和运输商品的筛选距离见补充材料表S3和表S10。比较计算涵盖第1、5、14和44周，共672小时、224个三小时时段。生产和库存决策采用三小时时段。在重新计算的配置中，氢气交付在每个三小时时段的供需两端保持平衡，各条路线在每周汇总为相同的路线合同量。GTL-GH与GTL-BH的天然气交付满足28个日平衡，每日包含8个时段。机场交付与需求采用周尺度。碳供给选项包括煤化工来源、天然气化工来源、工业捕集和直接空气捕集（DAC）；氢供给选项包括绿氢、副产氢和灰氢，通过情景指示参数启用或停用。模型考虑费托合成（FT）与甲醇制航空燃料（MTJ）两条合成路线29，路线模块的启用假设见表S5，原料、工艺和捕集参数见表S9；MTJ路线显式表示甲醇中间品库存。模型执行产能、物料流和库存上限，并通过短缺变量记录未满足需求。基准CTL情景在现有资源条件下无法满足90%的最低产量要求，其必要资源供给上界为78.6147%。部分供给诊断移除该项不等式并保留其余约束，固定该诊断的生产资产进行替代周测试，两个周组合采用相同的诊断服务范围。
